evidence/reviews/seattle-building-permit.reason: The source unit is the permit, but the dependence unit is the construction project or development site: the release itself states that permits sharing ParentPermitNum, RelatedMUP or a development site are correlated and that no row independence is claimed (README.md:58,67; construction.json:278,424). The project keys are not shipped: carry_columns is empty (construction.json:37) and the linking fields are reduced to presence flags (build.py:205-206), so permitnum, although unique (build.py:243-244), would treat sibling permits as independent. issueddate is a shipped non-predictor carry (build.py:31, absent from FEATURES at build.py:21-30), is the declared event key and split key (construction.json:36,70), and is the issuance event at which sibling permits of one project are commonly released together. In public train, a label-free same-day signature (issue day, ZIP level, class, type, description length, application-to-issue days) places 6.0% of rows in multi-permit groups, 48% of which carry parent_permit_flag=1 versus 3.4% elsewhere; 88% of those groups have a unanimous label versus 57% expected under independence (within-group ICC 0.68). Every such group nests inside one issue day, so issue-day clusters contain the observed sibling dependence plus any same-day administrative batch effect. Train label ICC by issue day is 0.022 at about 13 rows per day (design effect about 1.27); public validation gives 0.014 (about 1.15). Train has 856 issue-day clusters over 36 months and validation 625 over 24 months, so the 21-month holdout window should supply several hundred clusters. Chosen from source meaning plus public train and validation data only, before holdout scoring; no holdout rows or holdout metrics were inspected.
limitations: issueddate is an issuance-day block, not the project entity. The true entity keys (ParentPermitNum, RelatedMUP, address, contractor) are not in the released extract, so project-level clustering cannot be applied or verified.

Sibling permits issued on different days fall in different clusters. Among train rows with parent_permit_flag=1, a looser date-free signature finds 41 groups (123 rows) spanning different issue days (median span 258 days, maximum 975) with 76% unanimous labels, so some project dependence escapes this clustering and can cross split boundaries. That signature is a weak proxy and may include coincidental matches.

Issue-day clusters also pool unrelated permits issued the same day (median 12 rows per day, maximum 60 in train). This widens clusters beyond the project but does not restore independence across days.

Common shocks at month or year scale are not absorbed: train label rates drift by issue year (0.818, 0.752, 0.765) and outcome windows of train, validation and holdout overlap in calendar time. Intervals from issue-day clustering describe sampling within this regime, not transfer to another period.
Dependence through repeat applicants, contractors or sites over time is not captured; those identifiers were dropped from the release for terms-of-use reasons (README.md:55).
The holdout cluster count and cluster-size distribution are extrapolated from train and validation density and were not checked against holdout rows.

The same-day signature used as evidence is a heuristic built from shipped feature columns. It was used only to assess dependence, is not proposed as a cluster key, and true project membership was not verified against the raw source.

evidence/reviews/fra-form54-hazmat-relea.reason: The dependence unit is the physical accident event. Form FRA 6180.54 is a per-railroad, per-consist report, and the shipped rows are not strictly one per event: build.py:469-472 makes colliding composite keys (same railroad code, date, state, station, milepost, accident type) unique by appending a sequence suffix, so the uniqueness check at build.py:621-634 passes by construction. Public rows show 7 such suffixed pairs in train and 4 in eval, plus same-date/same-state/same-scene pairs that differ only in consist fields or railroad class. No shipped column identifies the event exactly, because railroad code, station and milepost are hashed into accident_id and then discarded (build.py:106-115,495). accident_date is the finest shipped column that is constant across every report of one event; the contract names it event_key_column and a non-predictor carry (construction.json:4-6,120), and because the split is on this date (build.py:491-493) a cluster can never straddle train, eval and holdout. It is a deliberate coarsening: accident_date plus stateabbr is nested inside it and was not chosen so the key stays valid if two reports of one event disagree on state. Chosen from source meaning, contract metadata and public train/eval structure before holdout scoring; no holdout row or holdout metric was consulted.
limitations: accident_date is a superset of the event, not an event identifier: unrelated accidents on the same day are merged (in train, 6,576 date clusters for 12,541 rows, 3,008 singletons, largest cluster 10 rows). This costs some efficiency, not validity.

Repeated-carrier and repeated-location dependence is not captured. The reporting railroad code, station and milepost are not shipped, and reporting_railroad_class has too few levels (one class holds roughly 80-88% of public rows) to serve as a cluster.

Calendar-level dependence across days (reporting-threshold regimes, the base-rate decline, multi-day weather) is not captured by day clusters; per-year results should be read alongside any clustered interval.
An event whose reports carry different accident dates (midnight straddle or entry error) would be split across clusters. Not checked.

That the paired rows are multiple reports of one accident is an inference from Form 54 meaning and public-row structure; the publisher data dictionary was not consulted and the pairs were not traced to source records.

Holdout cluster-size distribution is unknown because holdout rows were not read. Rows dated by the January 1 fallback (build.py:431-442) would pool into one cluster per year; no such spike appears in train or eval (16 and 11 January 1 rows).

The observed multi-report structure is small (about 0.1-0.2% of public rows), so clustered and row-level intervals are expected to be close; the key is declared for correctness of the independence assumption, not because a large effect is anticipated.

evidence.data_used: public train.csv and eval.csv only (no holdout, no raw source)

standardplan_null_among_unit_adding_perm.comparison: unit-adding permits with populated standardplan complete at ~0.75-0.86 in every half-year

numberreviewcycles_null.note: same rows also have null daysoutcorrections and totaldaysplanreview

.local/studies/seattle-building-permit-c.interpretation: A field that is blank for 19% of never-completed unit-adding permits but for 0.04% of completed ones, with the blank share rising toward recent cohorts, is most simply explained by the field being written or finalised after issuance (or wiped on cancellation) in the current snapshot. That is outcome-dependent information not available at the stated prediction time. It is not proven: no historical ledger exists, and the release itself says availability is assumed, not proven.
.local/studies/seattle-building-permit-c.action_taken: Task, target, features and evaluator left unchanged; features used as permitted by the release contract. Concern disclosed here and in REPORT.md with an ablation. Roughly 0.03 of validation AUC is attributable to these rows; the share may be larger on later cohorts if the blank share keeps rising.
.local/studies/seattle-building-permit-c.not_done: No repair of the dataset, no change of target, no access to holdout or raw source to confirm.
